analysis.one_liner: Adjusts capital gains taxes for inflation when stocks and business assets are sold.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Ways and Means Committee after being referred there in July 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the tax code so that when someone sells corporate stock or business property they have held for more than a year, the portion of the gain that just reflects inflation would no longer be taxed. To do this, it would raise the 'basis' — the value the tax code treats as the owner's original cost — by a measure of inflation, using the gross national product deflator. It sets special phased rules for assets held one to three years, excludes some kinds of property like options and preferred stock, and would apply to sales after the end of 1990.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors and business owners who sell assets held longer than a year, especially those who have held them a long time through periods of high inflation. Because ownership of corporate stock and business capital is concentrated among wealthier households, the tax savings would go mainly to them. Mutual funds and partnerships would pass the benefit through to their investors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Stock and business-asset investors, mostly wealthier households

how_it_helps.text: For any stock or business asset held more than a year, the bill replaces the adjusted basis with an indexed basis increased by the rise in the gross national product deflator since acquisition, so gains caused purely by inflation would no longer be taxed as real gain.

For assets held between one and three years, only a fraction of the inflation adjustment applies (one-third for one-to-two years, two-thirds for two-to-three years), phasing in the full benefit at three years.

The bill extends the same indexing through regulated investment companies, real estate investment trusts, common trust funds, partnerships, and S corporations, so investors in pooled funds would receive the benefit as well.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — and by extension all taxpayers — would bear the revenue loss from taxing only real (inflation-adjusted) gains. Under the tax system as it stood, ordinary workers paying income tax on wages could not get any comparable adjustment for inflation in their pay.

drawbacks.text: The benefit would flow almost entirely to holders of corporate stock and business capital, which is concentrated among higher-income households, while the revenue loss would be spread across all taxpayers.

The bill does nothing comparable for wages: an ordinary worker's income tax bill would not be adjusted for inflation under this provision, creating a two-track system in which investment income gets an inflation break that wage income does not.
Wage earners would indirectly bear the cost through the lost federal revenue, unless offset by other taxes or spending cuts, which this bill does not provide.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanism itself is a recognized policy idea: taxing inflation-driven gains means taxing a paper increase in value rather than real profit. But this version is one-sided — it gives the inflation break only to owners of stock and business assets, not to wage earners, and it raises no offsetting revenue. The distribution of the benefit toward wealthier households and the cost toward the general Treasury are the honest price of the proposal.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in July 1991 and the committee never acted on it, so it expired when that Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. John J. Rhodes III introduced the bill on July 10, 1991, with 10 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in its history.
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died in committee without receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the tax code stayed as it was: the Treasury kept collecting tax on inflation-driven gains, and no revenue was shifted away from capital-asset holders. Nothing about the outcome changed anyone's taxes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury kept the status quo tax treatment

for.name: Rep. John J. Rhodes III
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 10, 1991 and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans; the bill drew no Democratic support and died in a committee led by a Democrat.

industries.industry: Investors in corporate stock and business capital
industries.note: The bill would let these asset holders exclude inflation-driven gains from tax, a benefit that accrues mainly to wealthier households; the revenue given up would otherwise be spread across all taxpayers.

industries.industry: Mutual funds, REITs, and other pooled investment vehicles
industries.note: The bill includes pass-through rules so these funds and their investors would share the inflation-indexed basis benefit, making the break available through ordinary investment products.
